title: A student's clay tablet from about 1700 BC gives √2 to six decimal places

cover.alt: Both faces of a small, round, palm-sized clay tablet; one shows a square with its two diagonals and wedge-shaped cuneiform numbers.
cover.credit: A. Urcia, Yale Peabody Museum · CC0

body: **YBC 7289** is a small round tablet, probably made in southern Mesopotamia between 1800 and 1600 BC. It shows a square with both diagonals, and along one diagonal a number written in base 60: 1;24,51,10. That works out to about 1.414213, the square root of 2, off by less than one part in 2 million. It is the equivalent of six decimal digits, which scholars have called the greatest known computational accuracy anywhere in the ancient world. The student who scratched it probably copied the value from a table of constants, but other Babylonian tablets show a step-by-step method for computing such roots.

slides.alt: The front of the tablet with modern labels added: 30 on the side of the square, 1 24 51 10 along the diagonal and 42 25 35 below it.
slides.caption: The side of the square is labelled 30. Along the diagonal is √2 in base 60, and below it the diagonal of a square of side 30.
slides.credit: A. Urcia, Yale Peabody Museum; labels Theodor L. Franklin · CC0

slides.heading: Reading base 60
slides.text: Babylonian scribes counted in sixties, as we still do with minutes and seconds. So 1;24,51,10 means 1 + 24/60 + 51/3,600 + 10/216,000, which is 1.41421296… The true value of √2 is 1.41421356…

slides.heading: Match each digit to its place
slides.explanation: Each place is worth 60 times less than the one before it, just as each decimal place is worth 10 times less.

slides.label: how far the tablet's value is from the true √2
slides.text: The Greek astronomer Ptolemy used exactly the same base-60 value many centuries later in his Almagest, without saying where it came from.

steps.label: Copy √2 from a table of constants

slides.heading: Where's the point?
slides.text: Babylonian numbers had no mark showing which digit stood for units. So the 30 might really mean 30/60, a half. Read that way, the diagonal number is about 0.70711, which is 1 divided by √2. Historians aren't sure which reading the student intended.

slides.question: Why do historians think a student, not a master scribe, made this tablet?
options: It's small, round and boldly written
It is signed with a child's name
slides.explanation: Its small round shape and large writing match a "hand tablet", held in the palm for rough work. The arithmetic itself is excellent.
